judgments.description: One judgment per provision id listed in the document, in the order given.

clause_id.description: The provision id, copied exactly from the square brackets.

issues.description: Every construction issue this provision carries, one entry each, with its own probability. TWO SEPARATE QUESTIONS. (1) Is there an entry at all? That turns only on whether you can say what is wrong. If you can name a defect, list it however unsure you are that it matters, with a LOW probability (0.08, 0.15, 0.20); uncertainty goes into the probability, never into silence. If you can name nothing, return an empty list -- which is the ordinary answer, since only a small minority of provisions ever become the subject of a construction dispute. (2) Given a non-empty list, how long is it? That turns on how many SEPARATE defects you can name. Normally exactly one. Two issues of one type, or issues of both types, are the exception -- give them only when the extra defect is obvious and carries a genuinely high probability of its own, and never to keep the two types balanced. A type with no entry is read as probability 0, which is what it means: nothing specific was found of that type.

issue.description: Two sentences naming THIS specific defect: for risk type 1 the ambiguous term or the general-vs-specific tension; for risk type 2 the other part of the instrument this one has to be read against, named. Never empty and never null -- an entry exists only because there is a defect to name. If you cannot name one, write no entry.

type.description: Where the trouble lies. 1 if it is inside THIS provision's own words -- a term that can be read more than one way, a writing mistake, a general term whose reach against its own list is unclear -- however many cross-references it takes to show it. 2 if it is in how this provision stands with another part of the instrument: the two cannot both be given effect, or what this one means only settles once they are read together, or a recital pulls against the operative terms. Type 2 is not only direct conflict. The test: suppose the other provision did not exist -- if this one would STILL be in doubt, the trouble is here and it is type 1, and citing another provision as evidence of what a word HERE means does not change that; if the doubt would disappear because each provision read alone says something definite, it is type 2. Another way to the same line: a relational defect makes a court reach for a canon -- harmonise the two, give effect to every provision, avoid surplusage, or hold them irreconcilable -- while an intrinsic defect needs no canon, only the quoted words and the two rival readings of them. The words ambiguous, plain meaning, reasonable interpretation and read together fit both types and settle nothing.

prob.description: Probability in (0, 1] that a court would have something to construe on account of THIS issue. Greater than zero: the entry exists because the defect does, and a defect you would put at 0 is one you should not have listed. Low values are expected and are where most named issues belong -- 0.08 or 0.15 on a defect you can name but would not bet on is the right answer, not a reason to omit the entry. Two decimal places, on a 0.01 grid (0.03, 0.17, 0.62) -- do not round to the nearest 0.05 or 0.1. The range is stated here and not as minimum/maximum, which structured output rejects on a number; the reader clamps it.
